title: Compound Components
description: Use the compound component pattern with TypeScript to build flexible, expressive component APIs where parent and child components work together seamlessly.

data.text: **Compound components** are a set of components that work together to form a complete UI. Think of a `<select>` and `<option>` — they are meaningless alone but powerful together. The compound component pattern lets you build this relationship in React with full TypeScript support.
Compound components allow you to express a set of subcomponents that implicitly share state, making the API both flexible and intuitive.

The pattern uses React Context under the hood to share state between a parent and its children. The parent manages the shared state, and each child component reads from context. TypeScript ensures each child receives exactly the props it needs.

terms.definition: A group of components where a parent implicitly shares state with its children via context.
Mechanism where child components access parent state without explicit prop drilling.
State managed by the parent and automatically available to children without manual prop passing.
The way components are composed and used — compound components create a declarative, HTML-like API.

data.text: A Tabs component is the classic example. The parent holds the selected tab index. Each Tab knows whether it is active. Each Panel renders conditionally. All without passing any props explicitly between them.

data.title: TypeScript Enforces Correct Usage
data.text: The useTabsContext hook throws an error if a Tab or Panel is used outside Tabs. TypeScript also ensures the index prop is a number, and HTMLAttributes are correctly typed on Tab and Panel.

data.title: Exercise: Accordion Component
data.description: Build an Accordion compound component with Accordion, AccordionItem, AccordionTrigger, and AccordionContent. Each item shows its content when its trigger is clicked. Use context to track the open index, and allow only one item open at a time.
steps: Define AccordionContextValue with openIndex and toggle function
Build the Accordion parent that creates the context
Build AccordionTrigger that renders a button with an arrow icon
Build AccordionContent that shows/hides based on openIndex
Attach Trigger and Content as Accordion.Trigger and Accordion.Content
data.expectedOutcome: A fully working accordion where the consumer writes declarative JSX with <Accordion><AccordionItem> blocks, and only the active item's content is visible.

items.question: Why not just pass an openIndex prop to each item?
items.answer: You could — but the consumer would need to manage state and pass the same value to every child. Compound components hide that complexity by sharing state implicitly through context.

items.question: Can I use compound components with data from an API?
items.answer: Yes. Fetch data in the parent, pass it through context, and children can render different states (loading, error, success) based on what they read from context.

items.question: What about accessibility?
items.answer: Use proper ARIA attributes: role=tablist on the parent, role=tab on tabs, aria-selected on active tabs, and role=tabpanel on panels. TypeScript ensures these are strings when needed.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Compound components use context to share state implicitly
The parent creates state, children consume it via a guard hook
Static properties (Tabs.Tab) create a clean declarative API
TypeScript enforces correct nesting and prop types
data.takeaway: Compound components give you an API that reads like HTML — intuitive for consumers, powerful under the hood.
